legend: For any integer x%%ZSMJ0%%, define f(x)%%ZSMJ1%% as follows: f(x)=(x−1)⊕x⊕(x+1)%%ZSMJ2%% where ⊕%%ZSMJ3%% denotes the bitwise XOR operator.
We call an array [b1,b2,…,bm]%%ZSMJ4%% good if it satisfies the following condition: f(b1+b2+⋯+bm)=f(b1)+f(b2)+⋯+f(bm)%%ZSMJ5%%
You are given an array a%%ZSMJ6%% of length n%%ZSMJ7%%. Determine the number of good subarrays.
input: The first line of input contains an integer t%%ZSMJ8%% (1≤t≤104)%%ZSMJ9%% — the number of testcases.
The first line of each testcase contains a single integer n%%ZSMJ10%% (1≤n≤2⋅105)%%ZSMJ11%%.
The second line of each testcase contains n%%ZSMJ12%% integers a1,a2,a3,...,an%%ZSMJ13%% (1≤ai≤109)%%ZSMJ14%%.
It is guaranteed that the sum of n%%ZSMJ15%% over all testcases does not exceed 2⋅105%%ZSMJ16%%.
output: For each testcase, print the number of good subarrays.
note: In the first test case, there are 3%%ZSMJ17%% good subarrays [a1]%%ZSMJ18%%, [a2]%%ZSMJ19%%, and [a3]%%ZSMJ20%%.
